criterion_notes.c1: Examines domestic drinking and household water service delivery (in-house piped connections and public standpipes) across four small towns in Karnataka and Tamil Nadu, India.
criterion_notes.c2: Satisfies BOTH the plain wording and the narrow 2026-10-13 rule-type reading of Criterion 2. Under the plain wording, the study compares public institutional and governance arrangements for urban water supply. Under the narrow 2026-10-13 reading, it directly examines public utility ownership/institutional responsibility structure governing service access (elected municipal Urban Local Body [ULB] distribution vs. state-level engineering para-statal utility [KUWSDB/TWAD Board] bulk supply and/or retail distribution), tariff and cost-recovery rules (free public standpipes vs. fixed monthly unmetered connection tariffs, bulk water pricing, and fee-recovery enforcement), and frontline administrative discretion, accountability, and informal access practices (grievance redressal mechanisms, lineman bribes/tips to release water during scarcity, and staff collusion in illegal connections).
criterion_notes.c3: Comparative mixed-methods empirical study using household surveys (N=300 in Nelamangala, N=600 in Ramanagara), slum standpipe pot surveys (N=41), household volumetric metering (N=5 and N=8), semi-structured household interviews (>20 per town), key-informant interviews with linemen, ULB staff, para-statal engineers, and town councillors, borewell pump discharge measurements, and municipal/utility financial and operational records.
criterion_notes.c4: Reports multiple service access outcomes: per-capita water supply adequacy (LPCD), household connection rates (% standpipe-dependent vs. in-house connections and sumps) and household consumption (LPCD), supply continuity/frequency across normal and summer seasons, public standpipe spacing/access burden, perceived water quality, and tariff affordability (Rs/month and Rs/m3).
criterion_notes.c5: Clearly identifies population and units of analysis (town, ward, and household levels across Nelamangala, Ramanagara, Kannampalayam, and Palladam in southern India), exposure (institutional service modality—ULB vs. para-statal bulk/retail roles, dual-sourcing, and tariff/cost-recovery rules), outcomes, and a comparative mixed-methods case-study design.

evidence_quotes.quote: We used this framework to carry out an inductive analysis by comparing water service delivery and governance in four small towns across two states (Karnataka and Tamil Nadu) in southern India.

In terms of the institutional arrangements for water service delivery: the towns in Tamil Nadu (Kannampalayam and Palladam) receive bulk supply of river water from a provincial para-statal agency, Tamil Nadu Water and Drainage Board (TWAD Board), but manage the distribution of this river and of GW on their own.
Third, in terms of charging for water supply, the supply at the public standpipes is free of charge, whereas in-house connections are charged at a fixed (unmetered) monthly rate.

At the same time, in Nelamangala, citizens reported having to pay some ‘additional amounts’ (tips or bribes) to the linemen to get water released during times of scarcity – clearly frontline staff taking unfair advantage of the high level of water scarcity in that town.
In addition, semi-structured or open-ended interviews were conducted with linemen (at least 5 in each town), mid-level and senior ULB staff including the chief executive officers
These are presented in Table 4, and show that households dependent on standpipes alone may be at 40 lpcd whereas those with in-house connections and sumps may be at 47–60 lpcd

raw_response.exposure: Institutional and technical water service modalities: public utility governance/distribution structure (elected municipal Urban Local Body alone vs. state para-statal bulk supply with ULB retail distribution vs. state para-statal managing both bulk supply and retail distribution), water source deployment (groundwater only vs. dual surface/groundwater sourcing), tariff and O&M cost-recovery rules, and frontline administrative accountability/discretion.
raw_response.outcome: Domestic water service adequacy (town-level LPCD), household connection status (% standpipe-dependent vs. in-house connection and sump ownership) and household consumption (LPCD), supply frequency and seasonal continuity, standpipe density, water tariff affordability (Rs/month and Rs/m3), perceived water quality, cost recovery, biophysical sustainability, and administrative responsiveness/grievance redressal.
raw_response.population_and_sample: Four small towns (populations ~15,868 to ~95,167) in Karnataka (Nelamangala, Ramanagara) and Tamil Nadu (Kannampalayam, Palladam), India; analyzed at town, ward, and household levels using household source-mix surveys (N=300 in Nelamangala; N=600 in Ramanagara), standpipe pot survey (N=41), household metering (N=13 total), semi-structured household interviews (>20 per town), and interviews with linemen, ULB officials, para-statal engineers, and elected councillors.
raw_response.rationale: This empirical mixed-methods comparative study evaluates how public utility institutional structures (elected local municipal bodies vs. provincial para-statal water boards managing bulk supply and/or local retail distribution), tariff and cost-recovery rules, dual-sourcing regimes, and frontline administrative practices shape household and town-level domestic water access, consumption (LPCD), connection equity, supply frequency, affordability, and grievance responsiveness across four south Indian small towns. It satisfies all inclusion criteria under both the plain wording and the narrow 2026-10-13 rule-type mechanism reading of Criterion 2.
raw_response.study_design: Comparative mixed-methods multiple-case study (combining household surveys, volumetric metering, pump discharge measurements, administrative/financial records, and qualitative interviews)
